summary: A satirical piece about volunteers in the fictional town of Everyburg who, led by Susan Strongarm and Carlos Community-Heart, fixed potholes, renovated a library and built a dog park while the council stalled with endless deliberation. It contrasts the speed of citizen action with the slow pace of policy change and asks what policies are for if they don't follow the will of the people.
one_line: Satirical account of Everyburg volunteers fixing potholes, a library and a dog park in 2023 while the town council stalled.
key_facts: On September 2, 2023, volunteers in the town of Everyburg decided to stop waiting for slow policy change and took action themselves.
The volunteers were led by Susan Strongarm and Carlos Community-Heart.
Everyburg's problems included crumbling infrastructure and the lack of dog parks, in a town known for its award-winning poodles.
The volunteers' resources were garden shovels, wheelbarrows, duct tape, determination and donuts, with community spirit described as a currency more powerful than cash.
On November 12, 2023, volunteers fixed Percy Pothole, a crater so large that children mistook it for a new playground feature; Carlos wielded a shovel.
The council had long promised to address Percy Pothole, but action was always 'under advisement'.
Susan Strongarm organized a book drive that turned into a library renovation to repair, repaint and rejuvenate the aging building; young Tommy Textbook took part.
Local officials were still 'looking into' budget allowances for digital archives while the library was being renovated.
By December 15, 2023, the volunteers turned an overgrown, unused lot into a dog park with newly installed gates after waiting for the local government to build one.
Council members responded with talk of 'fiscal responsibility' and 'future considerations', while elected officials deliberated on renaming streets after forgotten historical figures.
The piece asks 'What's the point of policies if they're not changing with the will of the people?' and concludes that perhaps less talking and more doing is the key to governance.
